lead: A MOSFET that is off still conducts a little. Below threshold the surface is weakly inverted, not empty, so the drain current falls exponentially with gate voltage instead of stopping. This subthreshold current, together with gate tunnelling, gate-induced drain leakage and junction leakage, flows all the time and sets the standby power of a chip. Designers compare processes by the subthreshold swing and the off current per micrometre of width, and these two numbers decide how low the threshold, and so the supply, can go.
prereq: You need: VT and its temperature shift from Threshold voltage and body effect, and DIBL from MOSFET scaling and short-channel effects.

blocks.text: For V<sub>GS</sub> below V<sub>T</sub> a few electrons still sit at the surface, their number set by a Boltzmann factor. They move by diffusion over the source barrier, not by drift, so the current depends exponentially on the gate voltage:

I<sub>VT</sub> is the current at V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>T</sub> for the given W/L (it scales with W/L); φ<sub>t</sub> = kT/q is the thermal voltage, 26 mV at 300 K; SS is the subthreshold swing, below. For V<sub>DS</sub> above about 3φ<sub>t</sub> (roughly 0.1 V) the last bracket is 1, so on a log-current plot the curve is a straight line. The law holds from a few tenths of a volt below V<sub>T</sub>; above V<sub>T</sub> the square law takes over, and in between (moderate inversion) the curve bends smoothly from one to the other.
The thermal voltage is written φ<sub>t</sub> here so that V<sub>T</sub> always means the threshold voltage.
The subthreshold swing is the gate voltage needed to change the current tenfold:

2.3 = ln 10; n is the body factor, 1.2 to 1.5 in a bulk device, because the depletion capacitance C<sub>dep</sub> shares the gate voltage with the oxide. Even with n = 1, SS = 2.3 × 26 mV ≈ 60 mV per decade at 300 K: no conventional MOSFET switches more sharply at room temperature. Typical values are 70 to 100 mV/decade, and SS grows in proportion to the absolute temperature.

The off current Ioff is the current at VGS = 0 and VDS = VDD, quoted per µm of width: Ioff = IVT·10−VT/SS. Each SS of extra threshold cuts it tenfold, and DIBL raises it because a high VDS lowers VT. Heat raises it twice over: SS grows with T and VT falls by about 1 to 2 mV/K.

sections.h3: Other leakage paths and how designers fight leakage

items: Gate tunnelling: electrons tunnel straight through an oxide thinner than about 2 nm, from gate to channel. High-k dielectrics give the same Cox with a thicker physical layer and cut it sharply.

GIDL (gate-induced drain leakage): with the gate low and the drain high, the strong field in the gate-drain overlap bends the bands so far that electrons tunnel from the valence to the conduction band. Electrons go to the drain and holes to the body, so current flows out of the drain terminal into the body.
Junction leakage: reverse-biased source-body and drain-body junctions pass a small thermally generated current, which also grows with temperature.

blocks.text: Static power is V<sub>DD</sub> × total leakage. The knobs: high-V<sub>T</sub> cells off the critical paths (multi-threshold libraries), switching off idle blocks with a header or footer transistor (power gating), reverse body bias in standby, stacked off transistors (the stack effect), and keeping the chip cool. More on this in the topic Low-power design and power management.

examples.question: A process has SS = 80 mV/decade and I<sub>off</sub> = 10 nA/µm with V<sub>T</sub> = 0.3 V. A designer raises V<sub>T</sub> by 100 mV. (a) By what factor does I<sub>off</sub> fall? (b) What is the new I<sub>off</sub>? (c) A block has 10 mm of total off-transistor width at V<sub>DD</sub> = 1 V; find its leakage current and static power before and after. (d) Find n, with φ<sub>t</sub> = 26 mV.
steps: (c) W = 10 mm = 10⁴ µm. Before: 10 nA/µm × 10⁴ µm = 100 µA, so 100 µW at 1 V. After: 0.562 × 10⁴ = 5.62 µA, so 5.6 µW.
examples.answer: Leakage falls 17.8 times, to 0.56 nA/µm; the block leaks 5.6 µA (5.6 µW) instead of 100 µA (100 µW); n = 1.34.

examples.question: For the original device (SS = 80 mV/decade at 300 K, V<sub>T</sub> = 0.3 V), the chip heats to 360 K. SS grows in proportion to T and V<sub>T</sub> falls by 1.5 mV/K. By what factor does I<sub>off</sub> grow?
examples.answer: I<sub>off</sub> grows about 36 times, from 10 nA/µm to about 365 nA/µm, for a 60 K rise.

traps: Keep the two V-T symbols apart: the threshold is V<sub>T</sub>; the thermal voltage kT/q ≈ 26 mV is φ<sub>t</sub>.
No bulk MOSFET has SS below about 60 mV/decade at 300 K; SS = 2.3nφt with n ≥ 1.
I<sub>off</sub> is per µm of width; total leakage scales with the total width that is off.
Leakage rises with temperature, through both a larger SS and a lower V<sub>T</sub>.
The subthreshold swing SS is not the scaling factor S of MOSFET scaling.

quiz.q: Define the subthreshold swing and give its room-temperature limit.
quiz.a: The gate voltage for a tenfold change of subthreshold current; at least about 60 mV/decade at 300 K, typically 70 to 100.

quiz.q: Why is 60 mV/decade a floor for a MOSFET at 300 K?
quiz.a: SS = 2.3nφt with n = 1 + C<sub>dep</sub>/C<sub>ox</sub> ≥ 1 and φ<sub>t</sub> = 26 mV, so SS ≥ 2.3 × 26 ≈ 60 mV/decade. The carriers cross the barrier by thermal diffusion, which sets that limit.

quiz.q: SS = 90 mV/decade and V<sub>T</sub> rises by 45 mV. By what factor does I<sub>off</sub> fall?
I<sub>off</sub> = 2 nA/µm and a chip has 50 mm of off width at V<sub>DD</sub> = 0.9 V. Find the static power from subthreshold leakage.
A bulk planar MOSFET is reported with SS = 55 mV/decade at 300 K. What would you suspect?
quiz.a: It is below the thermal limit, so the measurement is suspect (temperature, noise, a gate hysteresis artefact) or the device works by another mechanism such as band-to-band tunnelling. A conventional bulk device cannot do it.

quiz.q: Distinguish GIDL from gate tunnelling current.
quiz.a: GIDL is band-to-band tunnelling in the drain under the gate overlap, seen as drain-to-body current with the gate low. Gate tunnelling is current through the oxide itself, seen at the gate terminal.

beyond: Process design kits quote I<sub>on</sub>, I<sub>off</sub> and SS for every transistor flavour, and libraries mix high-, standard- and low-V<sub>T</sub> cells. Gate-all-around transistors bring SS close to the 60 mV/decade limit, and tunnel FETs and negative-capacitance FETs are research devices that try to beat it. Search for "steep-slope transistor" and "multi-threshold CMOS power gating".

figure.caption: Subthreshold current of the first worked example on a log scale. With a swing of 80 mV per decade the current falls tenfold for every 80 mV below threshold, so moving V<sub>T</sub> from 0.3 V to 0.4 V lowers the off current at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0 from 10 nA/µm to 0.56 nA/µm.
